doc.title: Bob Magnusson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Sarah Vaughan as a generous boss; Jimmy Cobb
summary: Vaughan was tough on club owners but loved her musicians. She paid for his flights, his wife and son's trip, and his move to LA. He compares working with her and Jimmy Cobb to graduate school.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: She was a wonderful boss. You know she had the nickname “Sassy” and she could be, and I saw her do it in the three years that I worked for her. But never, ever with any of us musicians. With club owners that would try to give her a hard time, or management, that kind of thing. I would see her go off on them. But she loved the musicians. And she did some absolutely wonderful things. My wife Janet and I had our son at that time. We have a son and three daughters, and at the time we just had our — and we were in New York, we’d just finished working at the Rainbow Grill and I think we’d been there two or three weeks, and we had about three or four days off, and then we were going to the Fairmont Hotel in Dallas to work for another two or three weeks. And Sarah one night, we were hanging out and she says, “Are you going to hang in New York with Jan” or with some friends I had. I said, “No, I’m going home to see my wife and son.” And she wasn’t obligated for that short of a time to fly me anywhere but from New York to Dallas and then after that home. Marshall Fisher, who she was living with, she said, “Marshall, get Bob a ticket to San Diego.” So she bought my ticket from New York back and she says, “Get yourself to Dallas.” So by the time I did all the flying I had about a day and a half to see the family. I get back to Dallas, and Sarah says, “Did you have a good time?” I said, “Yeah, just too short, I miss Janet.” And she says, “Would you like her and Matthew to come to Dallas?” I says, “I would love it.” She says, “Marshall, buy Matthew and Janet plane tickets.” She bought round trip, out of her pocket. She did wonderful — she wanted me to come to L.A., we had no savings, and this was in ’75 when I rejoined. I had a son and a daughter now and my wife was pregnant with our second daughter, the third child. And Sarah had called me to see if I wanted to rejoin. I said, “Yeah I really would.” It was right at a good time that I really wanted to come back. And she loaned us the money up front to get us up to L.A., and paid first and last rent and all that. I mean I have nothing but love and compassion — I’m beating up the microphone— a real special place in my heart for her. And then her singing was amazing. I mean she was great every night and then fantastic on other nights. I mean the consistency level was just amazing to me. And Jimmy Cobb also. Like between the two of them it was like going to graduate school or something for me, and I approached it like that. I says I realized I was lucky enough to be there with these people, take advantage of it, learn as much as you can. I thought if I can © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
get my groove with him, it’ll be in the right place. And he was just a sweetheart to me. I mean he is just a lovely, lovely man. I love him dearly to this day.
From Buddy Rich to Jimmy Cobb.
Yep. Opposite ends of the spectrum you know.
